title: Video Poker Strategy for Canadian Players in 2026
excerpt: Video poker rewards skill in a way slots cannot. Here is how Canadians should read paytables, choose variants, hold correctly and pick a sensible denomination.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
Video poker occupies an unusual position in the online casino lobby. It looks like a slot, sits beside the slots in most menus, and is played at the same solitary pace. Yet it is the one machine game where a player's decisions measurably change the outcome, which is why video poker strategy is worth learning in a way that slot strategy simply is not. A Canadian player who understands paytables and holding rules can find games returning close to 100 percent, while the player next to them, on the same screen, gives away several percentage points every hand without ever noticing.

The appeal is not that video poker is easy money. It is that the maths is visible. Everything you need to evaluate a machine is printed on the screen before you wager a cent, and that transparency is rare in a casino.

Why video poker is not a slot

A slot machine runs on a proprietary reel weighting that no player ever sees. You are told the return-to-player percentage, or sometimes you are not, and you have no way of verifying it or influencing it. The reels resolve on their own.

Video poker is built on a standard 52-card deck, occasionally with a joker added. The composition of that deck is known. The paytable is published on the machine. Because both inputs are fixed and public, the expected return of any given hand is calculable, and so is the expected return of the game as a whole assuming the player makes the best decision every time. That is the crucial distinction. Two people playing the same video poker variant on the same paytable will not get the same long-run return unless they play equally well.

It also means the house edge is not a single fixed property of the game. It is a property of the paytable plus your decisions. Change either and the number moves. Anyone coming to the format from online slots in Canada should treat that as the headline difference.

Reading the paytable before you play

The single most valuable habit in video poker is checking the paytable before the first hand. In Jacks or Better, the two lines that matter most are the full house and the flush, because those are the payouts operators most often trim.

The benchmark version is known as 9/6 Jacks or Better: nine coins for a full house and six for a flush, per coin wagered. Played with correct strategy, that game returns roughly 99.5 percent over the long run, which is among the best returns available anywhere in a casino. It is a well-established figure and a reasonable approximation to work from.

Reduce those two lines and the return falls quickly. An 8/5 version, paying eight for the full house and five for the flush, drops the return by roughly two percentage points. A 7/5 version costs you more again. Nothing else about the game changes. The graphics, the pace and the royal flush jackpot look identical, and a player who does not check the paytable will never know they chose the worse machine.

Two practical points follow. First, always compare paytables across the video poker section of a lobby rather than opening the first title you see. Second, be aware that the same nominal game may appear at multiple denominations with different paytables attached, and the better paytables are more often found at higher stakes.

The main variants worth knowing

Jacks or Better

The reference game, and the one to learn first. A pair of jacks or higher pays even money, and the strategy is the most forgiving to memorise. If you only ever learn one variant properly, make it this one.

Bonus Poker

A Jacks or Better derivative that pays enhanced amounts for four of a kind depending on rank. The full house and flush lines are usually reduced to fund those bonuses, so the total return is typically slightly lower than full-pay Jacks or Better, though the good versions remain strong.

Double Double Bonus

The most volatile of the common variants. Four aces with a low kicker can pay enormously, but the base hands are stripped back to pay for it. Two pair often returns only your stake, which changes the rhythm of the game entirely. Expect long flat stretches punctuated by rare large hands, and size your bankroll accordingly.

Deuces Wild

All four twos are wild. Full-pay versions can theoretically return marginally over 100 percent with flawless play, which is why they are increasingly rare and why the paytable deserves particular scrutiny. The strategy is genuinely different from Jacks or Better and must be learned separately; applying Jacks or Better instincts here is a costly error.

Joker Poker

Played with a 53-card deck including one joker as a wild card. The minimum paying hand is usually kings or better, and the strategy again differs meaningfully from the standard game.

Core holding rules and the mistakes that cost most

Every variant has its own optimal strategy chart, but a handful of principles apply broadly and correct the errors that beginners make most often.

  • Do not break a made hand to chase a bigger one. Discarding a card from a made flush or straight to draw at a royal is almost always wrong unless you already hold four to the royal. The value you give up exceeds what you are chasing.
  • Never keep a kicker. Holding a high card alongside three of a kind or two pair reduces your draw without improving your prospects. Take the full draw.
  • A low pair beats three to a flush in most spots. Discarding a paying-hand foundation to chase a suited draw is a classic beginner leak. The pair can improve to trips, a full house or quads.
  • A low pair usually beats holding two unmatched high cards. The pair already has value; two unpaired face cards do not.
  • Four to a flush beats a low pair. The exception that catches people out, and worth committing to memory.
  • Keep a single high card over nothing. With no pair and no draw, hold the highest card that can pair for a payout rather than redrawing five.

Beyond these, use a proper strategy chart for the specific variant and paytable. Most reputable charts are freely available, and there is no rule against keeping one open while you play online.

Always play maximum coins

On the standard five-coin machine, the royal flush pays a disproportionate bonus at five coins. At one to four coins the royal typically pays 250 coins per coin wagered; at five coins it jumps to 4,000. That single line accounts for roughly two percentage points of the game's total return.

The consequence is straightforward. Playing fewer than five coins does not reduce your risk in any meaningful way, it simply removes the best-paying outcome from your paytable. If five coins at a given denomination is more than you want to wager per hand, drop to a lower denomination and keep playing five coins. Never do the reverse.

Bankroll and denomination

Video poker is less volatile than a high-variance slot but more volatile than most people expect, because a meaningful slice of the return sits in hands you will rarely see. The royal flush arrives roughly once in 40,000 hands with optimal play, which for most recreational players means seldom.

Choose your denomination so that a five-coin hand is a small fraction of your session budget, then plan for several hundred hands. A useful reference point is to treat a session bankroll of 200 to 250 full bets as the minimum for a comfortable run on a low-variance game such as Jacks or Better, and considerably more for Double Double Bonus. If that arithmetic pushes you below the lowest available denomination, the sensible response is a shorter session rather than a reduced coin count.

Single-hand versus multi-hand

Multi-hand formats deal your held cards into several hands at once, each drawing from its own deck. The expected return per coin is identical to the single-hand version of the same paytable, so multi-hand is not better or worse value. What it changes is variance and speed.

Playing ten hands at once multiplies your wager tenfold and compresses a great many decisions into a short period. That accelerates both the swings and the rate at which the house edge is applied. Multi-hand suits players who already know the strategy cold and want faster action on a bankroll that can support it. Anyone still learning should stay on a single hand, where there is time to think through each decision. The same logic applies at a live table, as we discuss in our guide to online poker in Canada.

Loyalty and comp value

Because the house edge on a good video poker paytable is so thin, loyalty rewards represent a larger proportion of the return than in any other casino game. A game with a theoretical edge of half a percent, combined with a loyalty scheme returning a fraction of a percent in points, cash back or bonus credit, leaves a very small net cost.

Read the terms carefully, though. Many programmes award points at a lower rate on video poker precisely because the edge is thin, and some exclude it from wagering contribution entirely. That does not make the game a poor choice; it simply means the comp value you assumed may not apply. Checking how a specific operator treats the category is part of the evaluation we run in reviews such as our JackpotCity Casino review.

Putting it together

The workflow is short. Choose a variant you have actually learned the strategy for. Check the full house and flush lines before wagering. Pick a denomination that lets you play five coins comfortably for several hundred hands. Keep a strategy chart to hand until the decisions are automatic. Confirm how loyalty points apply.

Do those five things and you will be playing one of the lowest-cost games in the building. Skip the paytable check or the max-coin rule and you convert the same game into something no better than a mid-tier slot.
